summary: At just 2.2 square miles and roughly 3,300 residents, Nevada City packs a startling housing price tag — a median home value of $607,300 against a median household income of $69,552 yields a price-to-income ratio near 8.7, placing it firmly in territory where purchasing requires substantial savings or outside equity rather than local earnings alone. The town sits at about 2,500 feet in the western Sierra Nevada foothills, draped across forested ravines and creek-cut ridgelines that give its historic downtown — one of the most intact Gold Rush–era commercial strips in California — an almost vertical quality, with streets climbing steeply past Victorian storefronts, independent restaurants, and small galleries. Deer Creek runs directly through town, and the surrounding Tahoe National Forest puts genuine backcountry hiking minutes away, not hours. With nine hours of average daily sunshine and mild annual highs around 69°F, summers are warm and dry while winters bring actual cold and occasional snow — a rarity for a California town this small. Employment leans heavily on public-sector roles, tourism, and small businesses; this is not a job center, and most working residents commute out, often toward Grass Valley or down the hill toward Sacramento, roughly an hour-plus drive on winding Highway 49 and Interstate 80. Median rent at $1,756 consumes over 30 percent of that median income, underscoring a tight affordability picture on both the buying and renting sides. Nevada City is a place where the dramatic physical beauty and dense walkable core exist in genuine tension with the economic math of staying.
